Abstract

Ephemeral streams across the southern Great Plains move a disproportionate share of
regional sediment during brief, high-magnitude flow events, yet their transport
behaviour remains poorly constrained relative to perennial systems. This dissertation
combines three years of field monitoring at eleven gauged reaches with flume
experiments and a reach-scale numerical model to quantify how antecedent moisture,
vegetation density, and channel geometry jointly govern bedload flux. Field records
show that 68% of annual sediment yield occurs in fewer than nine hours of flow, and
that transport efficiency declines sharply where riparian grass cover exceeds forty
percent. Flume results reproduce this threshold and identify near-bed turbulence
suppression as the controlling mechanism. Incorporating the resulting parameterisation
into a one-dimensional model reduces predicted yield error from 41% to 12% across the
validation reaches. These findings suggest that regional sediment budgets built on
perennial-stream relationships systematically overestimate ephemeral contributions,
with implications for reservoir siltation forecasting and conservation practice siting
throughout the region.

Keywords: fluvial geomorphology; sediment transport; ephemeral streams; Great Plains;
bedload; riparian vegetation
